title: Predictive Headroom: hybrid routing and backpressure design
body:
Purpose and scope

This note captures a consolidated architecture proposal for capacity-aware routing and admission control that combines predictive \"headroom\" estimation with local token-bucket gatekeepers and queue-depth backpressure. Goal: keep tail latency within SLOs across hosted/dedicated/private deployments while maximizing GPU utilization and reducing unfair throttling across tenants and regions. This is intended for discussion with serving-runtime, platform-engineering, and SRE before a small pilot.

Why a new approach (short):
- Existing token-bucket gate (static refill rates) leads to oscillation when utilization changes rapidly.
- Queue-depth-only admission defers the problem to expensive retries and cross-region failover storms.
- Per-node admission without lightweight global coordination can create hotspots and head-of-line blocking in multi-region routing.

Core ideas (high level)
1) Predictive headroom estimator (PHE): short-horizon model that estimates available serving capacity per GPU pool (node or instance-group) for the next N seconds using recent GPU utilization, average per-request token consumption, and in-flight queue depth. PHE outputs a smoothed headroom value (requests/sec or tokens/sec) and an uncertainty band.

2) Local adaptive token buckets: every admission point (node agent + region edge) runs an adaptive token-bucket where the refill rate is driven by PHE for its local pool. Refill rate adapts every 500ms–2s depending on signal stability. Burst size allowed scales with estimated uncertainty (higher uncertainty -> lower burst).

3) Multi-level backpressure: fail-fast at the edge when global heuristics indicate capacity shortage, fallback to regional queues if the remote region is saturated, and progressive degradation (rate-reduce, reduce response size, switch to cheaper model variant).

4) Lightweight global lease/soft-quota: a control-plane service issues short-lived soft-quotas for large tenants and cross-region balancing tokens to avoid cross-region overcommitment. Soft-quotas are eventually consistent and used primarily for fairness during large bursts.

Key signals used (inputs)
- GPU_util_pct: rolling average and 95p over recent 30s windows per instance-type.
- queue_depth: per-worker request queue length and time-in-queue histogram.
- avg_tokens_per_request: model-level moving average (per route/model).
- in_flight: per-GPU counts of active KV-cache-using requests (important for memory pressure).
- observed_tail_latency: p95/p99 response time for the last minute; used for safety overrides.
- cold_start_rate: number of requests that caused model swap/restore in last X minutes.

Admission logic (summary)
- Edge router receives request with tenant, route, model_hint, region preferences.
- Query local PHE for target pool. If predicted headroom >= request cost -> pass to local token bucket check.
- Token bucket checks: if tokens >= cost, consume and forward; else reject/queue depending on SLA and retry policy.
- If local pool soft-quota is zero (soft-quota service says no), and request is high-priority tenant, try regional fallback; else reject with congested response.
- For queued requests, prefer shallow region-local queues with per-tenant fairness and time-based dequeueing.

Adaptive refill algorithm (pseudo):
- Every T (0.5–2s):
  sample utilization U, sample avg_tokens_per_request C, sample queue_depth Q, sample in_flight I
  headroom_r = max(0, (1 - U/target_util) * peak_req_capacity) * smoothing_factor
  uncertainty = clip(var(U over last window) + var(Q), min=0.05, max=0.5)
  refill_rate = headroom_r * (1 - uncertainty) / C
  burst_size = base_burst * (1 - uncertainty) + min_burst
  // apply rate capping by tenant-class + global CAP

Operational guardrails
- Safety caps: refill_rate never increases above hard_max derived from physical capacity.
- Emergency backoff: if p99 latency spikes > 2x SLO, immediately reduce refill_rate by 50% and shift to fail-fast at edge.
- Fairness: maintain per-tenant min quota (guarantee) when tenant has active reserved capacity.
- Starvation prevention: decayed priority bump for tenants waiting > wait_threshold (e.g., 3s).

Multi-region considerations
- Asymmetric capacity: PHE runs per-region, but we expose a region-aggregated view to the global router containing headroom and uncertainty. Router policy chooses local-first unless redirected policy (cost-latency tradeoff) favors remote region.
- Cross-region token transfers: do not transfer tokens; instead allocate short soft-quotas from central control plane for planned cross-region bursts to prevent overcommit.
- Failover storms: to avoid thundering herd when a region fails, control plane will provide an emergency ban window during which edge routers apply probabilistic shedding (sample-based) to reduce sudden load on fallback regions.

Failure modes and mitigations
- PHE misprediction (overestimate): triggers increased queue depth -> emergency backoff kicks in; bail to fail-fast quickly to avoid long tails. Also record telemetry for model re-training.
- Clock skew and delayed signals: rely on short-lived leases and conservative uncertainty margins; do not allow instantaneous explosion of refill_rate from delayed low-util signal.
- Network partition between control plane and agents: agents continue with last-known conservative refill_rate and increase uncertainty; use local heuristics until reconnected.

Metrics to track (dashboards)
- predicted_headroom (per-pool) + uncertainty band
- token_bucket_refill_rate, token_bucket_tokens (per-agent)
- queue_depth, time_in_queue P50/P90/P99
- per-tenant accept_rate, reject_rate, avg_latency
- cross-region_fallbacks and emergency_ban_events
- GPU_util_pct broken down by instance and model type
- cost_per_accepted_request (for Optimize integration)

Rollout plan (safe, staged)
1) Lab test with synthetic traffic - verify PHE stability across sinusoidal load, random bursts.
2) Canary in a single non-critical region for a small set of tenants (low traffic) with full telemetry and kill-switch.
3) Expand to multiple regions, enable soft-quota balancing for medium tenants.
4) Gradual default adoption, enable probabilistic shedding on large cross-region failovers.

Example config snippet (edge agent)
- T = 1s
- target_util = 0.82
- base_burst = 30 requests
- min_burst = 3 requests
- smoothing_factor = 0.6
- emergency_p99_multiplier = 2.0
- wait_threshold = 3s
- tenant_default_strategy = \"reject_on_no_tokens\"

Open questions / TODOs
- Best way to estimate avg_tokens_per_request for mixed prompt workloads? Per-route learning or per-tenant?
- How aggressive should uncertainty shrink over time after stable signals? (currently using simple exponential decay)
- Integration surface with Redwood Optimize: can Optimize recommend target_util and base_burst by route?
- Agreement on tenant soft-quota semantics during capacity rebalancing (how strict vs best-effort).
- Do we want a global circuit-breaker for model-variant downgrades triggered by queue_depth?

Appendix: quick pseudo for agent admission check
function admit_request(req):
  pool = map_request_to_pool(req)
  headroom, uncertainty = query_PHE(pool)
  cost = estimate_cost(req)
  if headroom < cost * 0.5:
    return reject(\"CONGESTED\")
  if token_bucket[pool].tokens >= cost:
    token_bucket.consume(cost)
    forward(req)
  else if req.priority >= HIGH and can_queue(req):
    enqueue(req)
  else:
    return reject(\"RETRY_OR_FAIL_FAST\")

Notes to reviewers
- This is intentionally pragmatic: we accept probabilistic, eventually-consistent coordination rather than strict distributed token accounting. Goal is to reduce SLO violations while keeping implementation complexity reasonable.
- Feedback wanted on uncertainty modeling, per-tenant fairness policies, and interaction with global rollout/Optimize signals.

End of note.
